newsitem.title: CHINA: China law stresses party control over the military.
newsitem.headline: China law stresses party control over the military.

text.p: China on Thursday moved to tighten its grip on the military with a draft law saying the army must pledge allegiance to the ruling Communist Party.
"The draft Defence Law...legalises the principle of 'the party commanding the gun'," Defence Minister Chi Haotian told the National People's Congress, or parliament.
"Insisting on the Communist Party leading the armed forces...is a basic guarantee for consolidating political power, social stability, ethnic unity and national security."
Some Chinese critics said the controversial draft Defence Law appeared to contradict the country's constitution.
Article 29 of China's constitution reads: "The armed forces of the People's Republic of China belong to the people."
But Article 19 of the draft Defence Law says: "The armed forces of the People's Republic of China accepts the leadership of the Communist Party."
Legal specialists said the constitution made clear the leadership role of the party and implied party direction of the army.
"There is no contradiction," said a legal specialist at the Central Party School, the main training ground for senior Communist Party members.
"The party's leadership over the army is a time-honoured tradition. The law merely makes past practice legally binding," he said.

On Tuesday, Jiang Zemin, chief of the Communist Party and head of the armed forces, called on the army to obey only the party, seeking to ensure his grip on power after the February 19 death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.

Chi said in his speech to parliament that the military's job was to "stop domestic armed rebellion and unrest that attempt to split the state, subvert the government and overthrow the socialist system.
"In future, we must be on alert and guard against Taiwan independence and other activities attempting to split the state," Chi said.
Beijing, which has viewed Taiwan as a rebel province since a 1949 civil war split the two sides, vows to attack the island if it tries to declare independence.
Taiwan has denied it wants independence and says it is committed to reunification, but only when democracy is installed on the mainland.
The three million-strong People's Liberation Army -- the world's biggest -- sparked concern across the region last year when it conducted missile tests and war games near Taiwan.
The army has also been called on to quell unrest along the nation's borders like the far western region of Xinjiang where Moslem separatists want to set up an independent state.
Xinjiang was rocked by three separatist bomb attacks on buses in late February, leaving nine dead and 74 injured.
Legal specialists also said that another key objective of the draft law was to clarify management of military assets.
The draft law says such assets belong to the state and that the State Council, or cabinet, along with the powerful Central Military Commission would direct their management.
The army, cashing in on the sweeping economic reforms that have allowed many Chinese to get rich, is now a huge conglomerate with interests ranging from weapons to hotels.
China will boost its defence budget for 1997 by 14.7 percent to 80.57 billion yuan ($9.7 billion) compared with last year's budget, Finance Minister Liu Zhongli has said.
The budgeted figure for 1997 marked an increase of 12.7 percent over actual spending in 1996.
Parliament was expected to pass the bill at its two-week annual session which is due to end next week.
